A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JDR research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained content to be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: V2 reports original synthetic and real-world node-classification experiments, spectral-clustering results, ablations and simulations in its main text and appendices.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds runtime measurements, MLP comparisons and edge signal-to-noise ratio analyses.

M1.justification: Section 2.3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same spectral decomposition, vector matching and interpolation, graph/feature synthesis, iteration and final update procedures. The revised theoretical model and additional downstream MLP experiments do not change JDR.

E1.justification: The cSBM scenarios and real-world dataset coverage are retained, including the additional heterophilic benchmarks and larger graphs. The new MLP, runtime and ESNR evaluations reuse existing datasets and task coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds MLP and MLP+JDR comparisons against the GNN configurations on real-world datasets in Tables 10–11, and adds MLP+JDR to synthetic comparisons in Figure 6. V2 already included an unprocessed MLP on cSBM. DIGL, FoSR, BORF and AMP-BP remain; GPS is discussed but not directly benchmarked.

E3.justification: New evaluations tune JDR using an MLP downstream model, measure ESNR, and time preprocessing plus GCN training/evaluation on 100 splits using a common A100 setup. Existing splits, benchmark metrics and tabulated hyperparameters remain unchanged; these are additional protocols rather than revisions to the original experiments.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.5.3 tests whether transferring graph information into features makes MLPs competitive with GNNs. New A.5.7 tests graph denoising through ESNR and examines its relationship to classification accuracy. These substantially extend the diagnostic evidence beyond the retained component ablations, sensitivity studies and spectral-clustering analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 100 random-split runs and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals using 1,000 resamples. Appendix A.9 retains ten independent trials with standard-deviation shading. The new classification results follow the existing confidence-interval practice.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial results in Table 5, Tables 10–11 and 16–17, and Figures 6 and 12. Examples include Cora accuracy of 50.79% for MLP versus 62.66% for MLP+JDR, and higher ESNR for DIGL than JDR on every tested homophilic dataset. These are newly reported comparisons; the original benchmark scores in Tables 2–4 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Proposition 1 and Appendix A.3 are substantially replaced. V2 analyzes two symmetric spiked GOE matrices with a common signal parameter and requires lambda > sqrt(2). V3 analyzes a Gaussian graph matrix together with rectangular noisy features, requires lambda > 1 and mu > sqrt(gamma), and develops a different perturbation argument for graph and feature label alignment.

C1.justification: The principal alignment, node-classification and rewiring-performance claims remain. Section 5 sharpens the novelty claim from the first generally applicable algorithm when features are available to the first joint graph-and-feature denoising method, explicitly asserting that no directly comparable method exists.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations of graph-to-feature information transfer, explains ESNR–accuracy disagreements through feature information, and discusses hyperparameter-dependent runtime tradeoffs. It also reframes comparison fairness in Section 5. One new interpretation is inaccurate: A.5.3 claims GCN+JDR beats MLP+JDR on three heterophilic datasets, whereas Table 11 supports two.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1.4 newly specifies the timing setup: an NVIDIA A100 with 80 GB, Python-process timing, and outputs/logging left enabled. Table 5 supplies detailed measured runtimes. The existing code-access information, hyperparameter tables and general hardware disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: V3 adds references supporting the revised random-matrix analysis and multiclass motivation. Section 4 and A.5.7 expand the relationship to Dong and Kluger's already-cited work by discussing GPS and ESNR, and add connections to link-prediction-based denoising. The principal positioning within preprocessing graph rewiring remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion receive focused rewriting, and the spectral motivation gains explanatory text. New appendix subsections organize the additional analyses, while the main section order and most existing prose remain. Equal-contribution and acknowledgment text are also added.

P2.justification: V3 adds five tables for runtime, MLP comparisons and ESNR, plus two corresponding comparison figures. Figure 2 is redrawn and its amplitude labeling and caption are revised. The conference template changes typography and headers, and numerous retained displays are repositioned without changing their reported benchmark values.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the connection between the method and its supporting evidence: Proposition 1 now treats rectangular features, MLP controls test the need for downstream graph processing, and runtime and ESNR analyses expose practical and interpretive limits. These address important gaps in v2's justification. The new three-versus-two win-count error in A.5.3 is a limited reporting defect that does not outweigh these gains.
